fertilizer.title: Fertilizer decision
fertilizer.planningNote: A sound recommendation begins with measured field data. This table shows what each input informs; it is not an application recipe.
fertilizer.soilAnalysisUse: Available nutrients, acidity, salinity and the need for liming.
fertilizer.plantAnalysisUse: Current nutritional status, including hidden hunger before visible symptoms.
fertilizer.targetDestinationUse: Expected nutrient removal; grain and whole-plant harvest are different.
fertilizer.fieldHistoryUse: What was applied, removed or returned to the soil.
fertilizer.textureWaterUse: Leaching risk and whether applications may need splitting.
fertilizer.diagnosisCaution: Visual symptoms are clues, not confirmation. Water stress, disease, insects or another nutrient can mask them.
fertilizer.maizeIntro: Average amounts removed by maize at different yields and harvest destinations.
fertilizer.extractedUnit: Yield in t/ha; nutrients extracted in kg/ha.
fertilizer.notDoseWarning: Extraction is not a fertilizer dose. A recommendation requires soil and tissue analyses, a yield target, regional calibration and a local agronomist.
fertilizer.onionIntro: Documented effects for onion only; do not generalize them to other crops.
fertilizer.nitrogenEffect: Longer cycle, thick neck, excessive foliage, more foliar disease and poorer post-harvest storage.
fertilizer.potassiumEffect: Can induce magnesium and calcium deficiencies.
fertilizer.phosphorusEffect: Can induce zinc and copper deficiencies.
fertilizer.scrollHint: Swipe the table sideways to see all nutrients.
fertilizer.botanicalIntro: When a source is available, this guide separates species data, validated group guidance and seasonal timing. A photo never defines a dose.
fertilizer.unknownGroupNote: There is no validated fertilizer guide for this plant group yet. The decision checklist remains available, but no group-specific rule or dose is inferred.
fertilizer.growthStressUse: Separate establishment, active growth, flowering or fruiting, and dormancy. Correct drought, waterlogging, damaged roots or a recent transplant before feeding.
fertilizer.labelHistoryUse: Confirm N-P-K, release type, label directions, the last application and whether the substrate already contains fertilizer.
fertilizer.plantNoDoseWarning: A photo alone cannot establish a safe dose. Follow the product label and local analysis; never copy a dose from another species, climate, pot or field.

pestManagement.samplingPlanUse: Define the unit, method, points and frequency for the crop and its growth stage.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.collectBody: This app lets you photograph a plant, tree, insect, mushroom, crop, fish or bird to identify it, and record an animal call to identify it by sound. Identification is done by AI services: Kindwise (plants, trees, insects, mushrooms, crops), Fishial.AI (fish) and Nyckel (birds). Sound is identified on our own server, so recordings never reach a third party. When NatureLens's privately managed, calibrated worldwide BioCLIP service is active, bird photos may be processed there first: photos remain only in memory during the request and are not retained. While it is disabled, or if it fails or cannot substantiate an exact species, the same photos may be sent to Nyckel with sample capture disabled, without a guarantee of ephemeral retention.
privacy.thirdPartyBody: When you take or upload a photo, that photo is sent to the matching identification service to produce a result. We do not store your photos on any server we control. To show you a reference picture and a description of the species, the app asks Wikipedia about the scientific name — Wikipedia therefore sees which species you looked up, but not who you are. Some vendors only write in English; translating that text, and asking the in-app specialist a question, sends that text to Anthropic.
privacy.localStorageBody: Your saved collection - identified species, notes, and timestamps - is stored locally on your own device using browser or app local storage, and it is never shared with other users. If you are a subscriber and sign in, the collection's text data (never your photos) is also synced to our server so it can follow you across devices; deleting your account removes it from our servers.
privacy.noAccountsBody: This app doesn't require an account to use - your device is given a random anonymous identifier (stored only on your device) so we can tell when its one free identification per category has been used. If you subscribe, Hotmart collects your email and payment details directly to process the charge - we receive your subscription status and email, linked to that same identifier, so we can restore your access. Subscribers can optionally sign in by email code or Google to sync their subscription and collection across devices; this is never required to use the app. On the web version we use basic analytics (Google Tag Manager and Utmify) to measure visits and subscriptions; we never sell personal data.
privacy.dataLossBody: If you clear your browser data or uninstall the app, your locally saved collection will be permanently lost, since nothing is backed up remotely.
privacy.contactBody: Questions about this policy can be directed to the app's developer.
privacy.locationBody: For plants, trees, insects, mushrooms and crops, the app can send roughly where and when the photo was taken, which measurably improves the answer: the same small brown mushroom means different things in Brazil and in Norway. The coordinates are rounded to about 1 km before they leave your device — enough to place a species, not enough to identify a building — and they are never stored by us. You can turn this off at any time under Profile, and identification keeps working without it. It is never sent for fish, birds or sound.

discover.title: Discover
discover.subtitle: Feed your curiosity about the natural world
facts: The Corpse Flower (Amorphophallus titanum) can grow over 3 meters tall and smells of rotting flesh to attract pollinators.
Bamboo is the fastest-growing plant on earth — some species add up to 90 centimeters in a single day.
A single honeybee visits around 5,000 flowers a day, yet produces only a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life.
Mushrooms are more closely related to animals than to plants — they share a common ancestor with us from about a billion years ago.
The oldest known living tree is a bristlecone pine in California, estimated at over 4,800 years old.
Sunflowers track the sun while young, but once mature they settle facing east — which warms them earlier and attracts more pollinators.
Some orchids mimic the appearance and scent of female insects so precisely that males try to mate with them, pollinating the flower by accident.
A dragonfly catches around 95% of the prey it chases — one of the highest hunting success rates of any animal.
Ants have been farming fungi for over 50 million years, long before humans invented agriculture.
The Amazon rainforest produces roughly 20% of the oxygen released by land plants, and much of its rain falls from water the forest itself exhaled.
Butterflies taste with their feet — they step on a leaf to know whether their caterpillars can eat it.
A honey fungus in Oregon spans nearly 10 square kilometers, making it one of the largest living organisms on the planet.
The peregrine falcon exceeds 300 km/h in a hunting dive, making it the fastest animal alive.
Fish do not have eyelids — most simply never close their eyes, even while resting.
The Venus flytrap counts: a trigger hair must be touched twice within about 20 seconds before the trap closes, so rain does not waste it.
Trees in a forest share nutrients through underground fungal networks — a mother tree can feed a struggling seedling metres away.
The Arctic tern migrates from pole to pole every year, covering more than 70,000 kilometers — the longest migration of any animal.
Coffee, chocolate and vanilla all come from plants that depend on animals for pollination — no bees or midges, no morning coffee.
Some cicadas stay underground for 17 years before emerging, all at once, in the billions.
A pineapple is not one fruit but dozens of berries fused together around a single core.
Owls cannot move their eyes — their eyeballs are tubes fixed in place, which is why they rotate their heads up to 270 degrees instead.
The seeds of the sacred lotus can germinate after more than a thousand years of dormancy.
Salmon return to spawn in the exact river where they hatched, navigating by smell across thousands of kilometers of open ocean.
Fungi were the first complex organisms to colonise land — long before any plant did.
Fig trees do not flower outwardly: each fig is an inside-out cluster of flowers, pollinated by a wasp that enters through a tiny hole.
A hummingbird's heart beats over 1,200 times per minute in flight, and it must eat every 10 to 15 minutes to survive.
The strangler fig begins life on a branch high in the canopy, sends roots to the ground, and eventually kills the tree that hosted it.
Moss has no roots — it absorbs water directly through its leaves, which is why it thrives on rock and bark.
The mantis shrimp sees with 12 to 16 colour receptors; humans have three.
Aspen groves are often a single organism: thousands of trunks sharing one root system, some over 10,000 years old.
Ladybugs eat up to 5,000 aphids in their lifetime, which is why gardeners release them instead of spraying.
The seed of the coco de mer palm weighs up to 25 kilograms — the heaviest of any plant.
Electric eels are not eels but knifefish, and their shock can exceed 800 volts.
Lichens are not one organism but two — a fungus and an alga living as one, able to survive in outer space.
The male emperor penguin balances a single egg on his feet through the Antarctic winter, going two months without eating.
Nettles sting through tiny glass-like hairs that break off in the skin, and the antidote often grows nearby: dock leaves.
Some deep-sea fish are transparent, using invisibility as camouflage where there is nowhere to hide.
A mature oak can drop 10,000 acorns in a good year, and roughly one in ten thousand becomes a tree.
Crows recognise individual human faces, hold grudges, and teach their young who to avoid.
The world's smallest flowering plant, a watermeal, is the size of a grain of sand — a dozen fit on a fingertip.

airPurifying.title: Air-Purifying Plants
airPurifying.desc: NASA studied these species for cleaning indoor air.
airPurifying.intro: In the late 1980s, NASA tested dozens of common houseplants to find which ones could help scrub pollutants from the sealed air of spacecraft cabins — and discovered that many everyday favorites are surprisingly good at absorbing toxins like formaldehyde, benzene, and carbon monoxide. This collection rounds up the species that performed best in that research and have since become classics of home air-quality lore. They're no substitute for opening a window, but a few well-placed pots are an easy, low-effort way to help freshen the air in the rooms you spend the most time in.

species.name: Snake Plant
species.note: One of NASA's top performers, converting CO2 to oxygen even overnight, unlike most houseplants.

species.name: Spider Plant
species.note: NASA ranked it among the best at scrubbing formaldehyde and xylene from ordinary household air.

species.name: Peace Lily
species.note: Topped NASA's original study for stripping benzene, formaldehyde, and trichloroethylene from indoor air.

species.name: English Ivy
species.note: NASA's highest scorer overall, prized for clearing formaldehyde and even airborne mold spores.

species.name: Boston Fern
species.note: A NASA-tested formaldehyde remover that also raises humidity in dry, heated indoor rooms.

species.name: Golden Pothos
species.note: Nearly indestructible and documented to filter formaldehyde, benzene, and carbon monoxide from indoor air.

species.name: Rubber Plant
species.note: A NASA Clean Air Study standout, steadily pulling formaldehyde out of everyday living spaces.

beginnerSucculents.title: Beginner Succulents
beginnerSucculents.desc: Low-water plants that thrive on a little neglect.
beginnerSucculents.intro: Succulents earned their beginner-friendly reputation honestly: their thick, water-storing leaves and stems let them shrug off a forgotten watering or two without sulking. This lineup leans into the toughest, most forgiving varieties out there — plants built to tolerate the classic rookie mistakes of overwatering, underwatering, and inconsistent light. Give any one of these a bright windowsill and a little patience, and you've got a nearly foolproof entry point into growing your own plant collection.

species.name: Jade Plant
species.note: Stores water in thick stems and leaves, so a missed watering or two won't faze it.

species.name: Snake Plant
species.note: Thrives on total neglect, tolerating low light and weeks of dry soil without complaint.

species.name: Zebra Plant
species.note: Stays compact and slow-growing, making it nearly impossible to overwhelm with too much care.

species.name: Aloe Vera
species.note: Forgives inconsistent watering thanks to gel-filled leaves built to survive drought on their own.

species.name: Panda Plant
species.note: Fuzzy, water-storing leaves shrug off dry spells, making this a nearly foolproof first succulent.

species.name: Burro's Tail
species.note: Plump trailing leaves hold their own water reserves, rewarding hands-off owners who resist overwatering.

species.name: Mexican Hens and Chicks
species.note: Classic rosette shape stores water efficiently and multiplies easily, forgiving beginners' inevitable missteps.

petSafe.title: Pet-Safe Houseplants
petSafe.desc: Non-toxic greenery for homes with cats and dogs.
petSafe.intro: Sharing a home with cats and dogs doesn't mean giving up on houseplants, but plenty of popular species are genuinely harmful if nibbled. This collection rounds up well-documented, non-toxic favorites, cross-checked against ASPCA safety data, so you can fill windowsills and shelves without worrying about a curious paw or an exploratory bite. From trailing vines to flowering favorites, each pick here earns its spot for being safe first and beautiful second.

species.name: Spider Plant
species.note: ASPCA-listed non-toxic to cats and dogs, and its cascading leaves give curious paws something safe to bat at.

species.name: Boston Fern
species.note: This lush, textured fern is non-toxic to pets, making it a safe way to add jungly volume to any room.

species.name: Parlor Palm
species.note: A classic Victorian houseplant that's non-toxic to cats and dogs, tolerating low light without posing any risk.

species.name: Prayer Plant
species.note: Its leaves fold up at night like praying hands, and it's completely safe if a curious cat takes a nibble.

species.name: Watermelon Peperomia
species.note: Compact and non-toxic, its striped leaves make a striking, pet-safe accent for shelves and side tables.

species.name: Zebra Haworthia
species.note: A pet-safe alternative to toxic aloe and jade, this striped succulent delivers the look without the risk.

species.name: African Violet
species.note: One of the few flowering houseplants confirmed non-toxic, so pets can share a windowsill with the blooms.

medicinalHerbs.title: Medicinal Herbs
medicinalHerbs.desc: Plants with a long history of healing uses.
medicinalHerbs.intro: Long before modern medicine cabinets, home gardens were the original pharmacy: herbs like lavender, peppermint, and echinacea have been grown, brewed, and applied for centuries to ease everyday discomforts. This collection highlights plants with well-documented roles in folk and traditional medicine systems around the world, from Mediterranean kitchen staples to Ayurvedic classics. Most thrive on a sunny windowsill, letting you grow a living piece of herbal history at home.

species.name: Aloe Vera
species.note: Its gel-filled leaves have soothed burns and minor skin irritations across cultures for thousands of years.

species.name: Lavender
species.note: Long prized for its calming scent, traditionally used to ease stress and promote restful sleep.

species.name: Peppermint
species.note: Menthol-rich leaves have soothed upset stomachs and headaches in folk medicine for centuries.

species.name: German Chamomile
species.note: Its daisy-like flowers brew into a gentle tea long used to calm nerves and aid digestion.

species.name: Purple Coneflower
species.note: Native to North America, its roots and flowers were used by Indigenous peoples to support immune health.

species.name: Rosemary
species.note: This fragrant Mediterranean shrub carries an ancient reputation for sharpening memory and aiding circulation.

species.name: Holy Basil (Tulsi)
species.note: Revered in Ayurvedic tradition for centuries, its leaves are steeped as an adaptogenic tea for stress.

species.name: Turmeric
species.note: Ayurvedic medicine has used this golden root for centuries to calm inflammation and support digestion and wound healing.

species.name: Ginger
species.note: Chinese and Ayurvedic healers have long chewed or brewed this rhizome to settle nausea and warm the digestion.

species.name: Ginseng
species.note: Prized in Traditional Chinese Medicine for over two thousand years as a restorative tonic for energy and vitality.

species.name: Ashwagandha
species.note: An Ayurvedic staple for millennia, its root is traditionally taken to ease stress and rebuild strength and stamina.

species.name: Elderberry
species.note: European folk healers have brewed its dark berries into syrups for centuries to fight colds and flu.

species.name: Valerian
species.note: European herbalists have dried this pungent root since ancient times as a traditional remedy for restless sleep.

species.name: Witch Hazel
species.note: Native American tribes distilled its bark and leaves into an astringent wash for bruises, swelling, and skin irritation.

species.name: Goldenseal
species.note: Cherokee and other Native healers used this bitter root to treat sores, infections, and digestive ailments.

species.name: Devil's Claw
species.note: Traditional healers of the Kalahari have long used this hook-fruited root to relieve joint pain and arthritis.

species.name: African Wormwood
species.note: One of southern Africa's most widely used traditional medicines, steamed or brewed to relieve coughs and congestion.

species.name: Yerba Mate
species.note: The Guaraní people of South America have long brewed its leaves as a stimulating, digestion-aiding daily tea.

species.name: Gotu Kola
species.note: Revered in Ayurvedic and traditional Southeast Asian medicine as a wound-healing herb said to sharpen memory and calm the mind.

species.name: Licorice Root
species.note: Used across Chinese, Ayurvedic, and Middle Eastern medicine for centuries to soothe coughs, sore throats, and upset stomachs.

species.name: Neem
species.note: Bitter neem leaves, bark, and oil are Ayurveda's classic remedy for skin eruptions, wounds, and parasitic infections.

species.name: Amla (Indian Gooseberry)
species.note: Richest natural source of vitamin C in Ayurveda, amla anchors rasayana tonics prized for rejuvenation and digestion.

species.name: Brahmi
species.note: Ayurvedic Medhya Rasayana herb traditionally taken to sharpen memory, calm the mind, and support learning.

species.name: Guduchi (Giloy)
species.note: Called Amrita, 'root of immortality,' this stem decoction is Ayurveda's go-to for fevers and building immunity.

species.name: Shatavari
species.note: Root tonic revered in Ayurveda as the premier female rejuvenative, traditionally used to support lactation and hormonal balance.

species.name: Arjuna
species.note: Bark powder long used in Ayurvedic cardiology to strengthen the heart muscle and support healthy circulation.

species.name: Haritaki
species.note: Called the 'king of medicines' in Ayurveda, this fruit anchors Triphala for digestion, detoxification, and elimination.

species.name: Bibhitaki
species.note: One of Triphala's three fruits, traditionally used in Ayurveda to clear excess mucus and support respiratory health.

species.name: Fenugreek
species.note: Seeds soaked and eaten across South Asian households to ease digestion, support lactation, and balance blood sugar.

species.name: Long Pepper (Pippali)
species.note: Pungent fruit in Ayurvedic Trikatu blends, traditionally used to kindle digestive fire and clear respiratory congestion.

species.name: Sandalwood
species.note: Cooling paste applied in Ayurveda to soothe inflamed skin, fevers, and calm the mind during meditation.

species.name: Indian Sarsaparilla (Anantamul)
species.note: Sweet-rooted vine used in classical Ayurvedic formulas to cool the blood, purify skin, and ease joint pain.

species.name: Bael (Bengal Quince)
species.note: Unripe fruit pulp is a traditional Ayurvedic staple for soothing chronic diarrhea and dysentery.

species.name: Guggul
species.note: Resin at the heart of Ayurveda's Guggulu formulas, traditionally used to manage cholesterol and joint inflammation.

species.name: Manjistha (Indian Madder)
species.note: Root long used in Ayurveda as a blood purifier for clear skin, wound healing, and lymphatic support.

species.name: Jatamansi (Spikenard)
species.note: Fragrant root long used in Ayurveda to calm the nervous system and promote restful sleep.

species.name: Astragalus
species.note: Huang qi root is decocted to fortify wei qi, boost stamina, and support wound healing.

species.name: Reishi Mushroom
species.note: Ling zhi mushroom was prized by Daoist herbalists to calm shen, ease insomnia, and lengthen life.

species.name: Dong Quai
species.note: Dang gui, the 'female ginseng,' has nourished blood and eased menstrual complaints for two millennia.

species.name: Goji Berry
species.note: Gou qi zi berries are steeped or eaten to nourish liver and kidney yin, brightening the eyes.

species.name: Schisandra
species.note: Wu wei zi, the 'five-flavor fruit,' astringes the lungs, calms the mind, and protects the liver.

species.name: Chinese Skullcap
species.note: Huang qin root clears damp-heat and has treated fevers, coughs, and dysentery since ancient formularies.

species.name: Rehmannia
species.note: Steamed di huang tonifies kidney yin and blood, a cornerstone ingredient of many classical formulas.

species.name: Chrysanthemum
species.note: Ju hua flowers are brewed as tea to clear heat, soothe red eyes, and ease headaches.

species.name: Japanese Honeysuckle
species.note: Jin yin hua flower clears heat-toxin and has long treated fevers, sores, and throat infections.

species.name: Chinese Cinnamon (Cassia)
species.note: Rou gui bark warms kidney yang and moves stagnant blood to relieve cold-type pain.

species.name: Poria
species.note: Fu ling, a fungal sclerotium, drains dampness, calms the spirit, and strengthens the spleen in decoctions.

species.name: Chinese Yam
species.note: Shan yao tuber tonifies spleen, lung, and kidney qi, traditionally simmered into tonic porridges.

species.name: Bupleurum
species.note: Chai hu root harmonizes the liver and disperses heat, key for alternating fever and chills.

species.name: Notoginseng
species.note: San qi root is applied to stop bleeding and bruising while invigorating blood circulation.

species.name: Codonopsis
species.note: Dang shen root serves as a gentler ginseng substitute, tonifying qi and strengthening digestion.

species.name: Fo-Ti (He Shou Wu)
species.note: He shou wu root is prepared to nourish liver and kidney, said to blacken graying hair.

species.name: Yarrow
species.note: Known as soldier's woundwort, used since antiquity to stop bleeding and speed healing of battlefield wounds.

species.name: St. John's Wort
species.note: European folk remedy for melancholy and nerve pain, its yellow flowers steeped in oil for wound-healing salves.

species.name: Sage
species.note: Latin salvere, to heal, reflects its age-old use gargled for sore throats and taken to ease digestion.

species.name: Thyme
species.note: Mediterranean cough and chest remedy, its volatile oils long used in syrups to loosen stubborn phlegm.

species.name: Marshmallow
species.note: Root and leaf mucilage soothed sore throats, coughs, and irritated gut linings across centuries of European apothecary use.

species.name: Pot Marigold
species.note: Bright petals crushed into salves to clean cuts and calm inflamed, slow-healing skin.

species.name: Milk Thistle
species.note: Mediterranean seeds traditionally chewed or brewed to protect and tonify the liver after heavy feasting.

species.name: Fennel
species.note: Aniseed-scented seeds chewed after meals to ease colic, bloating, and infant wind for generations.

species.name: Stinging Nettle
species.note: Stinging leaves brewed as a spring tonic tea to cleanse the blood and relieve joint aches.

species.name: White Horehound
species.note: Bitter Mediterranean herb boiled into candies and syrups as a classic remedy for coughs and bronchitis.

species.name: Comfrey
species.note: Nicknamed knitbone, its mashed root and leaves were poulticed onto fractures, sprains, and bruises for centuries.

species.name: Feverfew
species.note: Bitter-leaved herb chewed fresh or brewed as tea, a long-standing folk answer to migraines and headaches.

species.name: Mullein
species.note: Downy leaves and flowers infused into oil or tea for coughs, sore throats, and earaches.

species.name: Hawthorn
species.note: Berries, flowers, and leaves steeped as Europe's classic heart tonic for a failing or anxious pulse.

species.name: Linden (Lime Flower)
species.note: Fragrant flowers steeped as a calming tea to break fevers and soothe restless nerves.

species.name: Meadowsweet
species.note: Fragrant flowering herb long used for fevers and joint pain, later yielding the chemical blueprint for aspirin.

species.name: Osha Root
species.note: Root chewed or brewed by Rocky Mountain tribes like the Navajo and Ute to ease sore throats and respiratory infections.

species.name: Black Cohosh
species.note: Root used by Cherokee and other Eastern Woodland peoples to ease menstrual cramps and support childbirth.

species.name: Devil's Club
species.note: Inner bark used by Tlingit, Haida, and other Pacific Northwest Coast peoples to treat arthritis, infections, and diabetes symptoms.

species.name: Wild Bergamot
species.note: Blackfeet and other Plains tribes brewed leaf tea from this thymol-rich mint to treat colds and respiratory infections.

species.name: Bearberry (Uva Ursi)
species.note: Leaves brewed by numerous Native American tribes as a diuretic and remedy for urinary tract infections.

species.name: Slippery Elm
species.note: Cherokee and Iroquois peoples used the mucilaginous inner bark to soothe sore throats and heal wounds.

species.name: Cascara Sagrada
species.note: Pacific Northwest tribes dried and aged the bark of this buckthorn as a reliable natural laxative.

species.name: Cinchona
species.note: Andean Quechua peoples used the bitter bark to treat fevers long before it became the source of quinine.

species.name: Cat's Claw
species.note: Asháninka and other Peruvian Amazon peoples brewed this woody vine's bark for arthritis and immune support.

species.name: Coca
species.note: Quechua and Aymara peoples of the Andes have chewed the leaves for millennia to combat altitude sickness and fatigue.

species.name: Dragon's Blood
species.note: Amazonian peoples apply this tree's red latex sap directly to cuts and wounds as a natural antiseptic.

species.name: Pau d'Arco
species.note: Inner bark brewed as tea by Indigenous Amazonian peoples to treat infections, fevers, and skin conditions.

species.name: Boldo
species.note: Mapuche healers in Chile have long used boldo leaf tea to support liver function and ease digestion.

species.name: Copaiba
species.note: Amazonian peoples tap this tree's resin and apply it topically to wounds as an anti-inflammatory remedy.

species.name: Guarana
species.note: Sateré-Mawé people of the Brazilian Amazon domesticated this vine, roasting its seeds for sustained energy and focus.

species.name: Black Seed
species.note: Known as 'the seed of blessing' in Prophetic medicine, its oil treats asthma, digestive upset, and skin infections.

species.name: Frankincense
species.note: Tapped from Arabian trees for millennia, its resin treats joint inflammation, wounds, and respiratory complaints.

species.name: Myrrh
species.note: Harvested across the Horn of Africa and Arabia, its resin disinfects wounds and soothes sore gums and throats.

species.name: Senna
species.note: Egyptian physicians since antiquity have relied on its pods and leaves as a powerful, reliable laxative.

species.name: Hibiscus (Karkade)
species.note: Steeped as karkade across Sudan and Egypt, its calyces are a folk remedy for high blood pressure and fever.

species.name: Moringa
species.note: Long used across Sub-Saharan Africa, its leaves treat malnutrition and inflammation and support nursing mothers' milk supply.

species.name: Baobab
species.note: Africa's 'tree of life' yields fruit pulp and bark traditionally used against fever, diarrhea, and malaria.

species.name: Rooibos
species.note: South Africa's Khoisan and Cape Dutch settlers brewed this reddish bush as a remedy for allergies and colic.

species.name: Buchu
species.note: Khoisan healers in the Cape used its pungent leaves to treat urinary tract infections and kidney ailments.

species.name: Cancer Bush (Sutherlandia)
species.note: Known to the Khoi as 'kankerbos,' this Southern African shrub is a traditional tonic for stress, fatigue, and immune support.

species.name: Umckaloabo (African Geranium)
species.note: Xhosa and Zulu healers in South Africa used its tuberous root to treat coughs, bronchitis, and tuberculosis.

species.name: Hoodia
species.note: San hunters of the Kalahari chewed this spiny succulent to suppress hunger and thirst on long treks.

species.name: Henna
species.note: Beyond body art, Middle Eastern and North African folk medicine applies its leaf paste to treat fungal skin infections.

species.name: Mastic
species.note: Chewed since antiquity across the Eastern Mediterranean, this tree resin soothes stomach ulcers and digestive complaints.

species.name: Carob
species.note: Middle Eastern folk medicine ground its pods into a remedy for childhood diarrhea and digestive upset.

floweringPerennials.title: Flowering Perennials
floweringPerennials.desc: Blooms that return year after year.
floweringPerennials.intro: Flowering perennials are the backbone of a garden that keeps giving: unlike annuals, they die back in winter and regrow from the same roots, rhizomes, or tubers each spring. Many settle in and spread into fuller clumps over the years, so one planting can reward you with more blooms every season. This collection gathers well-loved, easy-to-find perennials that anchor beds and borders with reliable, repeat-blooming color.

species.name: Peony
species.note: Long-lived tuberous roots can bloom in the same spot for fifty years or more, largely undisturbed.

species.name: Daylily
species.note: Despite the name, each fan multiplies into thick clumps that flower reliably for generations.

species.name: Purple Coneflower
species.note: This prairie native returns from a sturdy taproot, self-seeding into ever-larger colonies over time.

species.name: Bearded Iris
species.note: Fleshy rhizomes spread just below the soil surface, splitting into new fans that rebloom each spring.

species.name: Black-eyed Susan
species.note: Spreads by rhizomes and self-seeding to form dependable golden drifts that return each summer.

species.name: Garden Phlox
species.note: Sturdy clumping stems die back to the roots each fall, then resurface fuller the next year.

species.name: English Lavender
species.note: Woody perennial stems survive winter dormancy and leaf back out to flower again every summer.

oceanAndRiverFish.title: Ocean & River Fish
oceanAndRiverFish.intro: From coral reefs to cold mountain rivers, these are the fish people most often photograph and ask about. Scientific names stay in Latin worldwide, so a name you learn here works on any coast.

species.name: Clownfish
species.note: Lives inside sea anemones whose sting it is immune to, trading protection for cleaning. Every clownfish is born male and the dominant one becomes female.

species.name: Rainbow Trout
species.note: Native to cold rivers of the Pacific coast and now farmed on every continent except Antarctica. Its pink flesh comes from the crustaceans it eats.

species.name: Atlantic Salmon
species.note: Hatches in freshwater, spends years at sea, then finds the exact river it was born in to spawn. Its species name means "the leaper".

species.name: Northern Pike
species.note: An ambush hunter that stays motionless among weeds then strikes in a fraction of a second. The duck-bill snout and rear-set fins are its giveaway.

species.name: Common Carp
species.note: Farmed for over two thousand years and now found on every continent but Antarctica — prized food in some countries, an invasive pest in others.

species.name: Blue Tang
species.note: A reef surgeonfish with a scalpel-sharp spine near the tail it flicks out in defence. Bright blue as an adult, bright yellow as a juvenile.

species.name: Largemouth Bass
species.note: The most targeted freshwater sport fish in the world. You can tell it from the smallmouth because its jaw extends past the eye.

species.name: Yellowfin Tuna
species.note: Crosses whole oceans and can hold its body warmer than the water around it, which is why it swims fast in cold depths.

species.name: Zebrafish
species.note: A small striped river fish from South Asia that became one of science's most studied animals — its transparent embryos let researchers watch organs form.

species.name: Red Lionfish
species.note: Beautiful and venomous, with spines that deliver a painful sting. Native to the Indo-Pacific and a serious invader in the Atlantic and Caribbean.

birdsOfTheWorld.title: Birds of the World
birdsOfTheWorld.intro: Birds are the wildlife most people can photograph from a window. These ten span six continents and are among the most widely recognised species on earth — good practice for a sharp eye.

species.name: Barn Swallow
species.note: The most widespread swallow on earth, breeding across the northern hemisphere and wintering in the south. Its deeply forked tail is unmistakable in flight.

species.name: House Sparrow
species.note: Followed humans out of the Middle East into nearly every city on the planet. Males wear a black bib; females are plain sandy brown.

species.name: Common Kingfisher
species.note: A flash of electric blue over slow rivers across Europe, Asia and North Africa. It dives head-first and can take fish from a metre underwater.

species.name: Peregrine Falcon
species.note: The fastest animal alive, exceeding 300 km/h in a hunting dive. Found on every continent except Antarctica, increasingly nesting on skyscrapers.

species.name: Great Blue Heron
species.note: Stands motionless in shallow water for minutes, then spears a fish with a strike too fast to follow. Flies with its neck folded into an S.

species.name: Rock Pigeon
species.note: The city pigeon, descended from cliff-nesting birds — which is why ledges and window sills suit it so well. Both parents feed the young on "crop milk".

species.name: European Robin
species.note: Bold enough to follow a gardener for turned-up worms. The orange breast is worn by both sexes and defended year-round with song.

species.name: Mallard
species.note: The ancestor of almost every domestic duck. The green-headed male is famous, but only the female makes the classic loud quack.

species.name: Scarlet Macaw
species.note: A large parrot of Central and South American rainforests that can live over fifty years and pairs for life. Its beak cracks nuts no other bird can open.

species.name: Emperor Penguin
species.note: Breeds through the Antarctic winter, the males huddling in the dark with a single egg balanced on their feet for two months without eating.

gardenInsects.title: Neighbours Underfoot
gardenInsects.desc: Ten common invertebrates, properly looked at
gardenInsects.intro: The ten animals here live within a few metres of most front doors, and nearly everyone has looked at all of them without ever being told what they were doing. Underneath the familiarity sits chemical warfare, folded origami wings, intercontinental navigation and an ant colony 6,000 kilometres long.

species.name: Seven-spot Ladybird
species.note: Squeeze one and it bleeds from its knees on purpose — a bitter yellow fluid that makes birds drop it.

species.name: Common Earwig
species.note: Its hindwings unfold to more than ten times their packed size, one of the tightest folds in nature — and it barely ever flies.

species.name: Common Pill Woodlouse
species.note: Not an insect at all but a crustacean — a land-living relative of crabs that still breathes with modified gills.

species.name: House Fly
species.note: It tastes with its feet, so it already knows what it has landed on before its mouthparts get there.

species.name: Garden Snail
species.note: It feeds by dragging a toothed ribbon across leaves, and grows replacement teeth from the back as the front row wears away.

species.name: Western Honey Bee
species.note: A queen mates in the air over a few days, never again, and lays from that stored sperm for the rest of her life.

species.name: Painted Lady
species.note: No individual completes the migration circuit; it takes roughly six generations to get from tropical Africa to Europe and back.

species.name: Cellar Spider
species.note: It hunts other spiders by plucking their webs like a trapped insect, then attacks the owner that comes to investigate.

species.name: Argentine Ant
species.note: Workers from Spain, California and Japan, thousands of kilometres apart, meet without fighting: they are treated as one colony.

species.name: Common Earthworm
species.note: Darwin spent his last years studying earthworms and published a book about them six months before he died.

fungiOfTheWorld.title: Neither Plant Nor Animal
fungiOfTheWorld.desc: Ten fungi that quietly run the world
fungiOfTheWorld.intro: Fungi sit closer to animals than to plants on the tree of life, and the mushroom you see is only the fruit of a network of threads spreading unseen through soil, wood or a living insect. These ten include the one that kills more people than any other mushroom, an organism covering nine square kilometres of Oregon, and the mould that started the antibiotic era.

species.name: Fly agaric
species.note: The red-and-white toadstool of every fairy tale is real, is poisonous, and contains almost none of the toxin that was named after it.

species.name: Death cap
species.note: Responsible for the large majority of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide, and cooking, drying or freezing does nothing at all to its toxin.

species.name: Button mushroom
species.note: White button, cremini and portobello are not three mushrooms but one species, separated only by strain and by how long it was left to grow.

species.name: Brewer's yeast
species.note: A single-celled fungus behind bread, beer and wine, and the first organism with a nucleus to have its entire genome sequenced, in 1996.

species.name: Zombie-ant fungus
species.note: It walks an infected ant to a specific height above the forest floor, makes it bite down and die there, then grows a stalk out of its head.

species.name: Dark honey fungus
species.note: A single individual in eastern Oregon covers roughly nine square kilometres, making it by area the largest organism ever measured.

species.name: Bitter oyster
species.note: A small, tough, fan-shaped gill fungus whose gills glow green in the dark, but only if it came from the right side of the Atlantic.

species.name: Penicillium mould
species.note: The blue-green mould that contaminated Alexander Fleming's plate in 1928 was only correctly identified as this species in 2011.

species.name: Amphibian chytrid
species.note: A fungus too small to see has driven more species toward extinction than any other disease ever documented.

species.name: Alba white truffle
species.note: It fruits entirely underground, has defeated growers for decades, and a single 1.5 kg specimen went for about US$330,000 at a charity auction in 2007.

fromFieldToPlate.title: Where Dinner Began
fromFieldToPlate.desc: Ten staples and where they really began
fromFieldToPlate.intro: Almost nothing on a plate grows where it was born. These ten crops were domesticated in river valleys, highland forests and swamps thousands of years ago, then carried across oceans until the biggest harvests ended up on the wrong continent entirely.

species.name: Maize
species.note: Its wild ancestor carries about a dozen kernels, each sealed in a stone-hard case — nothing like a cob.

species.name: Cassava
species.note: Domesticated on the edge of the Amazon, it now feeds more people in Africa than in South America.

species.name: Arabica Coffee
species.note: Arabica is not an ancient species but a natural hybrid of two other coffees, with startlingly little genetic variation.

species.name: Soybean
species.note: Most of the world's soy never reaches a human plate directly — it is crushed into oil and livestock feed.

species.name: Sugarcane
species.note: It was first grown in New Guinea as a stem to chew; sugar refining and ethanol came thousands of years later.

species.name: Bread Wheat
species.note: Bread wheat never existed in the wild — it appeared in farmers' fields when a cultivated wheat crossed with a roadside grass.

species.name: Asian Rice
species.note: Rice was domesticated twice on two continents — once beside the Yangtze, and again from a different wild grass in West Africa.

species.name: Potato
species.note: Every potato grown in Europe, Asia and Africa traces back to the highlands around Lake Titicaca.

species.name: Banana
species.note: Wild bananas are packed with hard, pea-sized seeds; the seedless fruit exists only because people keep replanting sterile clones.

species.name: Sweet Orange
species.note: The sweet orange is not a wild species: it is a pomelo-mandarin cross that has been copied by grafting ever since.

heardNotSeen.title: Heard Before Seen
heardNotSeen.desc: Ten animals you meet by ear first
heardNotSeen.intro: Most wildlife encounters begin as a noise coming from somewhere you cannot see. These ten — owls and frogs, a cicada, two singing insects, a monkey and a fox — are all far easier to find by ear than by eye, and every one of them is saying something specific.

species.name: Tawny Owl
species.note: The famous 'twit-twoo' is two owls talking: the female's sharp ke-wick answered by the male's quavering hoot.

species.name: Common Cuckoo
species.note: Only the male says cuck-oo; the female answers with a bubbling water-chuckle that sends small birds into a panic.

species.name: Common Nightingale
species.note: Sings hardest between midnight and 3 a.m., and only unpaired males do it — once a female stays, the night song stops.

species.name: European Tree Frog
species.note: A five-centimetre frog with a throat sac wider than its own head, and a chorus that carries close to a kilometre on a still night.

species.name: American Bullfrog
species.note: A roughly 200-hertz bass jug-o-rum that travels the better part of a kilometre over open water.

species.name: Ash Cicada
species.note: Sings only when hot enough: the chorus builds as the morning heats up and cuts out when a cloud crosses the sun.

species.name: House Cricket
species.note: The chirp is two wings sawing together — a scraper dragged across a file of over a hundred teeth, at around 4–5 kHz.

species.name: Great Green Bush-cricket
species.note: A dry, unbroken rattle from dusk until well after midnight, sometimes running for hours with no real pause.

species.name: Black Howler
species.note: The dawn roar carries up to about five kilometres through forest, among the loudest calls made by any land animal.

species.name: Red Fox
species.note: The winter scream usually blamed on vixens comes from both sexes, and it is a mating call rather than distress.

fiddleLeafFig.name: Fiddle Leaf Fig
fiddleLeafFig.water: Weekly; let the top 1-2 inches of soil dry out
fiddleLeafFig.overview: Native to the lowland tropical rainforests of West Africa, the fiddle leaf fig is prized for its large, glossy, violin-shaped leaves with dramatic veining that made it an interior-design icon. It's grown as a dramatic floor plant that can reach ceiling height indoors, but it's famously particular about consistency in light, water, and temperature.
fiddleLeafFig.funFact: In its native habitat, Ficus lyrata can grow into a full-sized tree over 40 feet tall with leaves nearly twice the size of the ones we see indoors, and it can even produce small, inedible figs pollinated by a specific species of fig wasp - something it essentially never does as a houseplant.

bostonFern.name: Boston Fern
bostonFern.water: Keep soil evenly moist; never let it fully dry out
bostonFern.overview: Boston fern is a lush, arching cultivar of the sword fern, a species found in humid tropical regions worldwide. Its feathery, cascading fronds made it a favorite for hanging baskets and shaded porches since the Victorian era, though it demands steady moisture and high humidity to stay happy.
bostonFern.funFact: The 'Bostoniensis' cultivar wasn't bred on purpose - it was a natural mutation discovered in 1894 in a shipment of sword ferns sent from Philadelphia to a Boston florist, and it was propagated from that single sport into the houseplant we know today.

jadePlant.name: Jade Plant
jadePlant.water: Sparingly; let soil dry out completely between waterings
jadePlant.overview: Jade plant is a hardy succulent native to the semi-arid regions of South Africa and Mozambique, recognizable by its thick, glossy oval leaves and woody, branching stems that give it a miniature-tree look. It's a beloved beginner plant and is often passed down as a family heirloom, sometimes nicknamed the 'lucky plant' in feng shui traditions.
jadePlant.funFact: Given the right conditions, jade plants can live for 50 to 100 years, and mature specimens will occasionally reward growers with clusters of small, star-shaped white or pink flowers, usually triggered by cool nights and a dry spell.

calathea.name: Calathea
calathea.water: Keep lightly moist with filtered or distilled water
calathea.overview: Native to the rainforests of Bolivia, this striking member of the prayer-plant family (Marantaceae) is grown for its oversized, rounded leaves striped in silvery and dark green tones. Like its relatives, its leaves rise and fold at night and lower again during the day, a movement called nyctinasty that makes it feel almost alive.
calathea.funFact: This species used to be classified as Calathea orbifolia, but in 2012 genetic and morphological research split most Calathea species off into the genus Goeppertia - though nurseries and plant lovers still overwhelmingly use the old 'Calathea' name.
